keyVerseText: And Festus said, King Agrippa, and all men which are here present with us, ye see this man, about whom all the multitude of the Jews have dealt with me, both at Jerusalem, and also here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb ἐντυγχάνω (entynchánō) is derived from the preposition ἐν (en, meaning 'in' or 'among') combined with τυγχάνω, which carries the sense of 'to happen upon' or 'to meet with.' This etymology reveals a root meaning centered on encountering or coming into contact with someone or something, often unexpectedly or by chance. Beyond the common English glosses like 'make intercession,' the literal sense of 'falling in with' or 'meeting' enriches the understanding of the verb as involving direct engagement or approach, whether in conversation, petition, or intercession.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, ἐντυγχάνω appears five times, consistently conveying the idea of engaging with others either by chance or purposefully. Its primary translations include 'make intercession' (three occurrences) and 'have dealt' (one occurrence), indicating both the act of petitioning on behalf of others and of encountering or negotiating with people. This range demonstrates the word’s flexibility to describe both incidental meetings and intentional advocacy, underscoring relational dynamics in human and divine contexts.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, ἐντυγχάνω highlights the vital role of intercession as a form of relational engagement that bridges human need and divine grace. Its root meaning of 'falling in with' someone suggests that intercession is not a distant or abstract act but an intimate, direct approach to God or others. This underscores Christ’s unique role as the ultimate intercessor who meets us where we are and pleads on our behalf. Recognizing this word’s depth enriches our appreciation for prayer and mediation as active, personal encounters that shape the believer’s faith journey and dependence on God’s mercy.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 25:24 states, 'And Festus said, King Agrippa, and all men which are here present with us, ye see this man, about whom all the multitude of the Jews have dealt with me.' Here, ἐντυγχάνω conveys the idea that the Jewish leaders have actively engaged or confronted Festus concerning Paul. The word emphasizes the relational and somewhat confrontational nature of their dealings, showing that they did not merely hear of Paul but came to Festus to petition or press charges. This enriches the verse by illustrating the intensity and directness of the opposition Paul faced.
